note.note:
ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure  
  – Acute central chest pressure (“someone sitting on my chest”) that began while kneeling in the garden ≈2 h ago; still present. No specific food, drug, or environmental trigger identified.  

• Symptom timeline and progression  
  – Sudden onset during light activity → persistent; associated symptoms unchanged since onset.  

• ENT symptoms (negative unless stated)  
  – Throat swelling/closure sensation: denied/not mentioned  
  – Voice change/hoarseness: not mentioned  
  – Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: not mentioned  
  – Nasal/ocular symptoms: not mentioned  
  – Stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea: shortness of breath present but no stridor  
  – Distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): none reported  
  – Ear/neck pain or swelling: none reported  

• Relevant past episodes and treatments  
  – First episode of chest discomfort; no prior similar events.  
  – Mild swelling reaction to aspirin in the past; has taken aspirin inadvertently with only mild reaction (no airway compromise). No epinephrine injections or ED visits for allergy reported.  

• Allergies and current medications  
  – Allergy: Aspirin → mild swelling reaction.  
  – Current medications: not documented.  

• Social context  
  – Lives alone; nobody else in the house at time of call.

Objective:
• Observable swelling: none noted on video.  
• Airway/breathing: mild shortness of breath; no noisy breathing or visible distress described.  
• Mental status: alert and conversational.  
• Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.  
• Companion present: none.

Assessment:
• Working clinical impression: Suspected acute coronary syndrome (myocardial infarction vs. unstable angina).  
  Evidence: central pressure-type chest pain lasting >2 h with radiation to left arm/shoulder, diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea; multiple cardiac risk factors (male ~60 y, smoker, hypertension, overweight, strong family history).  
• DDx reference (aligned with transcript):  
  1. Acute coronary syndrome – most likely (see evidence above).  
  2. Aortic dissection – less likely; hypertension and smoking present but pain described as pressure without back radiation.  
  3. Pulmonary embolism – possible but chest pain not pleuritic and no provoking factors.  
  No conflicting data between transcript and DDx.

Plan:
• Immediate actions  
  – Emergency services (ambulance) already activated; clinician remained on line until arrival.  
  – Patient instructed to keep front door open for paramedics and wait near entrance.  

• Patient instructions  
  – Remain seated, avoid exertion.  
  – Report aspirin allergy and reaction details to ambulance/hospital staff.  

• Escalation criteria/red flags (reinforced)  
  – Worsening chest pain, new shortness of breath, syncope, or any throat/airway symptoms.  

• Follow-up  
  – Hospital assessment with ECG and cardiac enzymes planned by EMS.  
  – Further outpatient evaluation (cardiology, cholesterol check, smoking cessation counseling) once acute event addressed.  
  – Allergy: consider formal evaluation of aspirin sensitivity and discussion of alternative antiplatelet strategies after acute event.  

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but clinically expected elements: home/regular medication list, vital signs, physical exam of cardiovascular and respiratory systems, documentation of auto-injector availability for known aspirin allergy, detailed allergy reaction timeline, prior anaphylaxis plan.  
● Transcript–DDx conflicts: none identified.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; occasional minor overlaps but clinically relevant information discernible.
